Our release has two steps in a fixed order: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets are never deleted during a release.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what browsers use to find assets. Once it changes, any browser that loads it immediately requests the files it names. If those files aren't uploaded yet, the browser gets 404s and the page breaks. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists when the switch happens. Because the new files have new, versioned names, uploading them doesn't affect anyone on the current release. Nothing references them until the manifest changes. This makes the manifest switch the single moment the release takes effect. If the upload fails partway, we stop, and users see no change.

**Why we keep the old assets:** A browser that loaded the previous manifest keeps requesting the files it named. This happens with lazy-loaded chunks, a later navigation in a single-page app, or a tab left open for hours. If we deleted those files at the switch, those users would get 404s in the middle of a session, even though nothing on their side is wrong. Keeping the old assets lets every client finish on the version it started with and pick up the new one on its next manifest fetch. It also makes rollback simple: point the manifest back at the previous names, and those files are still there.

**Why the versioned names matter:** Each release's files have their own names, so the new upload never overwrites a file that a live client might be fetching. The same names also let us cache assets aggressively. A given URL always serves the same bytes.

Each release goes out in two steps: we upload every new asset under a new versioned filename, and only then switch the manifest to point at those names. The old assets stay on the server.

The upload comes first because the manifest switch is what makes the release live. As soon as the manifest names a new file, browsers will start requesting it. If that file isn't uploaded yet, they get a 404 and a broken page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists when it goes live, so the switch is a single, safe cutover.

We keep the old assets because some browsers loaded the previous manifest before the switch. Those pages still reference the old filenames and keep requesting them as users click around or lazy-load chunks. If we deleted those files, those sessions would break mid-use. Versioned names let old and new assets sit side by side without overwriting each other. Old sessions keep working on the old set while new visitors get the new set.

Our release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets stay where they are.

The upload comes first so that every name the manifest references already exists the moment the manifest goes live. If we switched first, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that aren't uploaded yet, getting 404s or a half-broken page. Because versioned names never collide with what's live, uploading early has no effect on users until the manifest flips.

Every release goes out in two steps, and the order matters.

**1. Upload the new assets under versioned names.** Each changed file (JS bundles, CSS, images) gets a name that includes its version or content hash, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. Nothing references these files yet, so uploading them has no effect on what users see.

**2. Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest (or the HTML that loads the assets) is the only file that tells a browser which asset names to request. Updating it is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload happens first:** As soon as the manifest changes, browsers start requesting the names it lists. If those files aren't uploaded yet, users get 404s, which can mean a blank page, missing styles or broken scripts. Uploading first means every name the new manifest points to already exists when the switch happens. It also makes the switch a single change to one file, so the release goes live in one step instead of piece by piece.

**Why the old assets stay available:** A browser that loaded the previous manifest keeps using those older asset names, sometimes for a long time. Open tabs, back/forward cache, CDN or proxy caches, and service workers can all keep serving the old manifest. Many apps also load scripts and chunks lazily, for example when a user navigates to a new route. If the old files were deleted, those users would hit 404s in the middle of a session even though nothing is wrong on their end. Keeping the old assets lets every client finish with the version it started on, and the next full page load picks up the new manifest.

Keeping the old files also makes rollback cheap: pointing the manifest back at the previous names restores the previous release with nothing to re-upload.
